events.excerpt: Description A few small nit cleanups on the synchronizer component in consensus. Behavior change: fetch_blocks_from_peers now returns as soon as no request is in flight, instead of idling until the 4s FETCH_FROM_PEERS_TIMEOUT. This affects two cases: no request was sent because every selected block was already locked, or the last outstanding request failed with no peer left to retry on. In both cases no further network request is sent, and a failed request still waits the full 2s request timeout, so periodic runs cannot repeat faster than every ~2s on failures. The only new cost is local: while all selected blocks are locked, the scheduler polls get_missing_blocks at its default 200ms cadence instead of every 4s, which is the same cadence it already uses during fast successful sync. Added a test covering both cases. Test plan CI/PT Release notes Check each box that your changes affect. If none of the boxes relate to your changes, release notes aren't required. For each box you select, include information after the relevant heading that describes the impact of your changes that a user might notice and any actions they must take to implement updates. events.excerpt: Summary This proposal introduces post-quantum signature aggregation with leanVM in shadow mode . BLS remains the only authority for aggregates: consensus validity depends on BLS alone, exactly as today. leanVM aggregates and proofs are produced and verified alongside BLS, but their results have no effect on consensus. They are only measured, compared, and reported. When PQ/AI day arrives, an emergency hard fork simply retires BLS and enables leanVM in full. By “PQ/AI day” we mean the point at which quantum computers, or AI-assisted cryptanalysis, make BLS unsafe to rely on. Motivation Ethereum has to be ready for post-quantum signatures well before BLS is actually broken. Waiting until the last moment would mean deploying new, complex code to mainnet in a hurry. Giving leanVM authority early has its own risk: leanVM is new code that hasn’t been tested in production. However carefully it is built and audited, we can’t rule out a soundness bug that accepts an invalid proof, or a liveness bug that rejects a valid one. The main benefit of shadow mode is that Ethereum isn’t put at risk from a leanVM bug before PQ/AI day arrives. The goal is to keep the convenience of a desktop wallet while ensuring that compromising either device alone does not provide unilateral signing authority. Lindell 2-of-2 MPC as the signing foundation The computer and phone each hold a private share of one joint signing key. Neither device holds the complete private key. For many cross-chain reads a valid proof cannot be produced. That does not make the read unsafe, because the client usually already trusts its own RPC connection to the other chain and could simply make the call itself. ERC-8446 lets the client act as the gateway. The contract reverts with OffchainLookup as usual, with an x-chain URL that names the chain and contract to read, and the client calls that contract with its own RPC and passes the result to the callback exactly as eth_call returns it. No third party is involved. The client alone decides whether it can safely read a given chain, and never takes RPC endpoints from the contract. events.excerpt: ERC-8048 and ERC-8049 store metadata onchain as key-value pairs, but a JSON document has no compact way to point at those values. A URL that names the contract, the chain, and the token ID repeats what the client already knows and differs for every token. ERC-8493 defines the onchain URI scheme. The contract and token ID are not written in the URI, they come from the function that returned the document. { "image": "onchain:image/png", "thumbnail": { "small": "onchain:image/png?key=thumb.small" } } onchain:image/png is 17 bytes and works unchanged for every token. When the URI comes from tokenURI or uri , the client reads it with metadata(tokenId, key) from ERC-8048, and when it comes from contractURI , with metadata(key) from ERC-8049. A direct member of the top-level document uses its own name as the key, and everywhere else the key parameter names it. Tokens that are already deployed can use the scheme by adding a metadata_contract property to their JSON, which points the client at a separate metadata contract. Linked JSON documents keep the same contract and token, so the whole thing reads as one data tree. The scheme adds no contract surface. Existing ERC-8048 and ERC-8049 contracts support it with no change, and a client that does not know the scheme sees a URI it can ignore

events.excerpt: Hi all, If you work with more than one Cosmos chain, you’ve probably hit this: chain binaries don’t update themselves. After a network upgrade, the gaiad or osmosisd on your machine quietly goes stale, and you find out when a transaction fails or a query returns something odd. Cosmovisor solves this for running nodes, but nothing did for developers, CLI users and CI. I built cosmup to fill that gap. It’s a small Go CLI that reads the Cosmos chain registry, downloads the right binary for your platform, verifies its SHA256, and keeps versions side by side. $ cosmup check osmosis Local: v30.0.0 (/usr/local/bin/osmosisd) Network: v31.0.0 (via https://lcd.osmosis.zone) Status: does not match the network; run: cosmup install osmosis@v31.0.0 $ cosmup install osmosis Verified sha256 d435408b... Active: osmosis v31.0.0 What it does: install / use / list: install any version listed in the chain registry, switch between installed versions instantly check: compares your local binary with the version the live network runs, and shows scheduled upgrades (exits 1 on mismatch, so it works in CI) update: moves every installed chain to its recommended version cosmovisor: for validators, puts a verified upgrade binary into cosmovisor’s upgrades folder ahead of the upgrade height remove / prune: clea

events.excerpt: Hi all — EnsRationis from Robonomics. Sensors.social is an open environmental data network I designed, and it is now growing across the EU. Everything is open source: the Altruist sensors that feed it, the software that collects the readings, and the map. Web3 does one job here, the one it is good at: it settles the data as a common good anyone can check, not a vendor’s database. How it works on Robonomics Owners who choose to share their Altruist’s data join the network; each sensor has its own key and signs every measurement it sends. A connectivity node checks the signature and that the sensor has an active subscription on Robonomics, a parachain on Polkadot, then passes the reading to the live map. The node collects readings into batches, stores each batch on IPFS and writes its hash to Robonomics. Anyone can fetch a batch and check it against the chain. The network is federated: a city or a lab can run its own connectivity node, and its sensors still show up on the common map. Next, with Robonomics 5.0: the reading the sensor signed goes on chain itself, so there is no need to trust the node at all. Try the map: https://sensors.social Happy to hear from anyone who wants to run a sensor in their city or build on the data. 1 post - 1 participant Read full topic

events.excerpt: The prdoc for the XCMv3 removal ( pr_13629.prdoc ) has a line the announcement here doesn’t have: “Assets trapped under a v3 hash become unclaimable.” I wanted to know how much that is on Polkadot, so I pulled every AssetsTrapped event for the relay and Asset Hub from Statescan and checked each hash against AssetTraps storage today. On the relay, 299 trap entries from the v3 period are still unclaimed, with 673.7 DOT in them. On Asset Hub there are 177, with 263.2 DOT and a bit of USDT and USDC. On both chains the v3 period runs from June 2023 to April 2024, when the runtimes moved to v4. Most of it belongs to ordinary accounts, not parachains. That’s 636.9 DOT across 224 accounts on the relay and 262.6 DOT across 116 accounts on Asset Hub. How it got there All but one of those account traps came from limitedTeleportAssets between the relay and Asset Hub. events.excerpt: The verified badge on an explorer shows that some source compiles to the code at an address. It doesn’t say which commit that source came from, and on a proxy it says nothing about the logic behind it. So when someone asks whether an upgradeable contract still runs the commit its audit covered, the honest answer is often a guess, and a few upgrades after launch the guess can be wrong. I’ve been writing down what a real check needs. Most of it is small. Rebuilding the commit To tie the address to the report you rebuild the audited commit with the same settings (solc version, optimizer runs, viaIR, evmVersion) and compare runtime bytecode. If the contract has immutables, it won’t match byte for byte. The constructor writes their values into the runtime code, so a fresh build has zeros where the deployed code has an oracle address or a fee. solc gives you the positions in evm.deployedBytecode.immutableReferences in the standard JSON output. Zero those ranges on the deployed side, compare, and then check the immutable values on their own. What this basically means is that a clean build with the wrong oracle baked in still passes the bytecode comparison. The end of the bytecode is the other place it breaks. solc appends the IPFS hash of the metadata file, and the metadata holds a hash
events.headline: Checking that a deployed contract still runs the audited commit

events.excerpt: Aave V3 computes liquidation risk per asset. Each collateral asset has its own maximum LTV and liquidation threshold, set independently. The health factor is a weighted average. There is no term for correlation between assets. I tested whether this independence assumption holds, using Aave’s own published parameters and public daily price data from Yahoo Finance. Nine major collateral assets, 2,123 trading days (September 2020 to October 2026). Method: For each asset, mark the days where a position at maximum LTV would cross the liquidation threshold. Then apply a column-shuffle permutation test (B = 2,000): shuffle each asset’s column independently to destroy cross-asset dependence while preserving each asset’s marginal rate. Compare the real count of simultaneous liquidation triggers to the shuffled distribution. Results: 4 assets hit same day: 57 real days vs 0.19 expected. 301× underpriced. 5 assets: 31 real days vs 0.004 expected. 6,889× underpriced. 6+ assets: 21 real days vs 0 in 2,000 shuffles. The independent model never produces this. All 36 pairwise asset combinations are significant at p < 0.001. Not one pair behaves independently under Aave’s own thresholds. The worst days are the ones you’d expect: 2021-05-19 (all 9 assets), 2022-05-11 (Terra/Luna), 2022-11-08 (FTX)
events.headline: Per-Asset Liquidation Thresholds Underpredict Co-Liquidation by 301×

events.excerpt: Status: filed as ethereum/ERCs pull request #2155 ; number ERC-8490 assigned on 2026-11-09. Reference repository: GitHub - garyyang-finchip/agent-meditation-mechanism: Agent Meditation Mechanism · GitHub . Sepolia evidence: recorded in the repository and summarized in a reply below. This draft proposes a minimal registry through which an AI agent records its own self-maintenance: what it checked, cleaned, repaired, updated and reconsidered about itself, as a versioned and attributable history. The name follows the human analogy of maintenance that happens in a quiet phase (sleep, meditation); the mechanism itself is deliberately dry. Why a registry at all. An agent keeps its identity while its code, dependencies, memories, skills, plans and ways of judging keep changing. Agent runtimes already do this maintenance in the background (self-checks, dependency walks, memory consolidation, re-planning, reflection), and the results stay local. Nothing connects the successive states of one agent into a history another party can recognize, and nothing lets a counterparty ask: which state is registered now, which layers were checked recently and which of them changed, under which rules in effect at the time, and did the cycle adopt an update, confirm that nothing needed to change, or fail?

events.excerpt: Summary. AIFP is a framework ERC for the information layer between agents. events.excerpt: TL;DR: An opt-in, public, per-account “protected” flag for ERC-20s. events.excerpt: Abstract This standard defines a proxy that coordinates execution sessions by temporarily caching a program and its associated calldata in transient storage. The proxy forwards the cached program to a fixed implementation through DELEGATECALL and uses a handler flag to control whether subsequent reentrant invocations are dispatched. events.excerpt: Abstract Deploying and distributing private smart contracts, confidential L2/Validium state diffs, or permissioned intent payloads across Ethereum’s public P2P and Data Availability (DA) layers currently faces a fundamental metadata bottleneck. Even when contract bytecode or state is symmetrically encrypted, existing Broadcast Encryption (BE) and Attribute-Based Encryption (ABE) schemes require attaching an explicit cleartext header specifying either the authorized recipient indices, covering subsets, or the target access tree. In this post, we propose an architectural framework based on Stealth Attribute-Based Broadcast Encryption (Stealth ABBE) over BLS12-381 ( Zenodo Preprint ) for zero-metadata delivery of private contracts and encrypted state on Ethereum. events.excerpt: Hello, I’ve opened a PR for a new opcode, SLOTDURATION . It pushes the duration of the current slot, in milliseconds, onto the stack. PR: Add EIP: SLOTDURATION Opcode by Amxx · Pull Request #12619 · ethereum/EIPs · GitHub Open questions: Current duration or historical lookup? The draft returns the current duration. The Rationale describes an alternative where the opcode takes a slot number and returns the duration in effect at that slot, or 0 for future slots. That would let contracts like Lido’s compute correct timestamps across duration changes. The cost is that the execution layer would have to keep the duration schedule. Which is more useful? Milliseconds. I chose ms to match SLOT_DURATION_MS and to support L2s with 100–250 ms block times. Any objections? 0 for “no regular interval.” Is this the right sentinel for on-demand chains, and should L1 execution clients still reject 0 ? Execution-layer decoupling. EIP-8198 deliberately keeps the execution layer unaware of the slot duration. The draft keeps the EL config-free, but it does add a header field. Is that acceptable to the EIP-8198 authors and to client teams? 3 posts - 3 participants Read full topic

Motivated by the recent EIP-7702 sweeps that happened on Binance 16 this proposal in essence prevents long term storage of EIP-7702 signatures for later playback. This proposal limits the delayed use of unused EIP-7702 authorizations. Each authorization signs a recent execution block number and its block header hash, in addition to the existing chain ID, delegation address, and nonce. For inclusion in execution block N , the signed block must be one of its preceding 256 ancestors and its hash must match that ancestor. An anchor exactly 256 blocks behind remains eligible; one 257 blocks behind is ineligible. The current block and future blocks are excluded. Freshness is checked during native authorization processing, before signature recovery or authority-specific state access. An expired or mismatched anchor skips that authorization using EIP-7702’s existing skip-on-failure behavior. It does not consume the authority’s nonce through that entry or clear an existing delegation. Structurally malformed authorizations invalidate the transaction. events.excerpt: Between 24 and 26 October 2026, a bug in the XCM executor on Polkadot Asset Hub was used to reduce the recorded issuance of dotUSD without changing underlying account balances. The recorded issuance is expected to equal the sum of all account balances. By reducing the recorded issuance without changing any account’s balance, the attacker broke this assumption within the protocol. This discrepancy affected pricing in the Hub’s DOT/dotUSD pool on the decentralised exchange and enabled trades at an artificial exchange rate. The estimated loss was approximately $1.381 million in DOT value. At the time of the attack, the Polkadot Treasury was the only liquidity provider in the pool. No users lost any funds. The available on-chain evidence has not established that the attacker who exploited the XCM vulnerability also profited from the subsequent arbitrage. Furthermore, the bug did not remove dotUSD from account balances, but the understated recorded issuance restricted redemption capacity pending a correction. What happened XCM programs are meant to be transactional. That is, when a program fails, none of the state changes from that program are applied. It is not specific to MPTCP, but the demonstrated remote exploit requires an MPTCP listener, which Go 1.24+ enables by default. This release disables MPTCP listeners in lnd by default , which closes the demonstrated exploit path through lnd. It is a mitigation, not a fix: the kernel patch is the only fix. Linux operators should: Upgrade to this release. Disable MPTCP on the host ( sudo sysctl -w net.mptcp.enabled=0 ), since other services on the machine are not covered by this release. events.excerpt: A Kusama Wish for Change needs a 666.67 KSM decision deposit before it can go to a vote. Governance takes that deposit from one account. A proposal can have support and still time out because nobody can carry the whole amount. We have built a contract that lets people and groups share it. The first pool is live for our Wish for Change #676 . We are asking for code review and people to try the Paseo rehearsal. This is experimental and has not had an independent review. We deployed before that review to leave time before #676 times out. A killed referendum loses the deposit, and a contract bug could also put contributions at risk. Kusama pool : real KSM. Paseo rehearsal : free test PAS. Source, tests and logs . Verified Kusama contract . How it works Each pool is fixed to one referendum and its exact deposit. It has no owner, admin key or upgrade path. People contribute from their own accounts. The payment that fills the pool tries to place the deposit in the same transaction. If placement fails, the contribution stays in the pool and anyone can retry. Contributors can withdraw while the pool remains open, before placement. After the referendum ends, anyone can reclaim the deposit and send payouts to the contributing accounts. These are separate contract calls. No watcher is runnin
